on efficacy more complete.
7. Olink units of concentration in serum should be clarified (normalised to what?)
Response: Thank you for broaching the subject. Olink's NPX (Normalised Protein eXpression)
is a relative quantification unit, log2-transformed and normalised to internal controls,
background levels to ensure comparability across runs, but it does not represent absolute
concentration. That is, the assay quantified protein expression levels using normalised log2-
transformed arbitrary units, with elevated values corresponding to increased protein abundance.
Several other studies using Olink to detect plasma proteomes have also used NPX as a relative
reference value with no actual concentration, such as Temba's study published in Nature
Medicine6 and Xie's study published in STTT7. Specifically, the raw data were normalised and
NPX values were calculated using Olink NPX Signature (version 1.16.0). Accordingly, the
description of normalisation is presented in the Methods section, which we hope will satisfy
your requirement for rigor in the article.
8. Are there diagnostic biopsies to determine PD-L1. If so this and the infiltration by T cells at
diagnosis would be important.
Response: This is a matter of great importance. We acknowledge the critical importance of
tumour microenvironment dynamics. A key translational limitation of this trial is the inability
to acquire paired tumour biopsies pre- and post-treatment, which precludes direct assessment
of therapy-induced immune remodelling in late-line HCC. As hepatocellular carcinoma is often
clinically diagnosed without biopsy, only 11/21 patients had archival tissue (diagnostic
biopsies/surgical specimens) available for analysis.
Immunohistochemistry revealed no significant correlation between pre-treatment PD-L1
CPS scores, CD8+/CD4+ T-cell infiltration densities, and clinical response to the therapeutic
regimen (P > 0.05; Figure R5; revised Figure S4B-S4C and Table S6). Crucially, most samples
were obtained during initial diagnosis—prior to any systemic therapy—and may have been
altered by subsequent front-line treatments, potentially obscuring true microenvironmental
associations.
We concur that serial tissue sampling is essential to decipher predictive biomarkers. Future
trials incorporating on-treatment biopsies (with rigorous ethical safeguards) are needed to
identify actionable immune signatures for precision management of anti-PD-1-refractory HCC.
Figure R5. PD-L1, infiltration of CD8+T and CD4+T cells are plotted and compared between
Rs and NRs, as well as CBRs and NCBs. Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to identify
significant differences.
9. The seminal work regarding immunotherapies for HCC should be referred to.
Response: We appreciate the insightful suggestion regarding seminal immunotherapy studies
in HCC. Key foundational works have been incorporated into the Introduction and Discussion,
including: 1) IMbrave1508 (atezolizumab/bevacizumab), ORIENT-329 and CARES-31010 for
establishing first-line standards; 2) Predictive biomarkers of PD-1 inhibitor efficacy, such as
inflammatory gene signatures (Sangro et al., J Hepatol 2020)11, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio
(NLR)12, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR)13, and the CRAFTY14 score—most
comprehensively reviewed by Llovet et al.15 A number of predictive biomarkers of PD-1
inhibitor efficacy have been identified, including inflammatory gene signatures11, neutrophil-
to-lymphocyte ratios (NLR) 12, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratios (PLR)13, and CRAFTY scores14.
A comprehensive review of this subject can be found in the work of Llovet et al.15; 3)
Mechanistic insights into immunosuppression, including in neoantigen processing and
recognition16, suboptimal priming/activation of tumour-specific T cells17,18, insufficient T-cell
expansion or co-stimulatory signals, impaired trafficking of effector T cells to tumour sites19,
inadequate cancer cell recognition by T cells, and the presence of T-cell inhibitory molecules
or immunosuppressive cells within the TME20.
These additions contextualise our study within the evolving HCC immunotherapy
landscape. Should any critical omissions be noted, we welcome guidance to further strengthen
the scientific discourse.
10. More background on RT for HCC should be given.
Response: We apologise for the omission of both the quotation and the background details from
the introduction. The revised References 19-22 and the relevant part of introduction delves into
the application of radiation therapy, with a particular emphasis on the use of SBRT in the
management of HCC. Due to an oversight in the original manuscript, the term "hepatocellular
carcinoma" was not qualified, which resulted in a misinterpretation. To rectify this, the
statement has been meticulously corrected in the revised manuscript, and a review on the
application of SBRT in HCC has been appended. The assistance rendered in the revision of the
manuscript is greatly appreciated.
11. A review on HCC immunotherapy should be referred to.
Response: Thank you very much for your valuable suggestion. While we have detailed several
phase III trials of immunotherapies, a comprehensive review of immunotherapies for HCC has
not been properly cited. We refer to Llovet's review (Immunotherapies for hepatocellular
carcinoma. Nat Rev Clin Oncol 19, 151–172 (2022). Ref. 3 of the revised manuscript) in the
reference part, and we are confident that it will make our manuscript more convincing.
12. Previous experiences of antiangiogenics with radiotherapy should be discussed across
diseases and specifically for HCC.
Response: This is a very bright suggestion. We reviewed the latest literature and found a recent
study published in the Red Journal (Sheng et al., 2025, Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys)
demonstrating that anti-angiogenesis may potentiate the distant effects of the combination of
radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma21. Furthermore,
Kashiwagi, S. et al. had previously reported that anti-angiogenesis promoted radiosensitivity in
glioma cells22 (Nature Medicine, 2008). The addition of these citations in the revised manuscript
reinforces the scientific validity and rationale of our study, and again, thank you for your advice
on refining the citations.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
I have read with great interest the study by Tang et al.
Their manuscript presents a phase 2 trial investigating SBRT combined with sintilimab (anti-
PD-1) and a bevacizumab biosimilar (IBI305) in patients with ICI-refractory HCC. The study
demonstrates a 33.3% ORR, a median PFS of 6.2 months, and an estimated median OS of 24.4
months. Furthermore, the study provides longitudinal biomarker analysis, identifying IFN-γ,
IL-6, and IL-2 as key cytokines associated with therapeutic response.
This work is clinically relevant and mechanistically insightful, with several limitations I have
detailed below.
1. Without a control arm (e.g., ICI + Bevacizumab without SBRT), it is unclear whether SBRT
directly contributes to improved outcomes. I would recommend to explicitly acknowledge this
limitation in the Discussion.
Response: We deeply appreciate your constructive feedback and acknowledge this limitation
regarding the absence of a control arm. As explicitly stated in the revised discussion section: "
Our study has inherent limitations. The single-arm design and modest cohort size (n = 21) —
though statistically predetermined by Simon's two-stage phase II framework — constrain
statistical power for subgroup analyses and may impact generalizability." This limitation is
further contextualised with other constraints (e.g., lack of serial biopsies) in the designated
discussion subsection.
2. Due to the limited sample size, it is difficult to assess the clinical reproducibility of the ORR
33%. In particular, in their sample size calculation, the authors mention that the alternative
hypothesis is ORR=40%. The study achieved an ORR of 33.3% - does this make the study
positive or negative? It is not clear from the discussion and it should be clarified.
Response: We appreciate the reviewers' constructive comments. Although the observed
ORR of 33.3% is clinically meaningful in second- or third-line treatment, it failed to meet the
predefined threshold of 40%. Our study design was established in 2022, referencing
contemporaneous data from immunotherapy, the ORIENT-32 study, and efficacy rates from
previous radiotherapy studies incorporating abscopal effects. We aimed to validate efficacy
exceeding expectations with a limited sample size, hence setting the threshold at 40%. However,
emerging data from 2024 indicated that the ORR for the ICI-resistant group receiving
regorafenib plus pembrolizumab in a prospective trial range from 5.9% to 11.1%23, suggesting
our initial 40% projection may have been too optimistic. While the expectations were not met,
this remains an encouraging approach, and we have revised the limitations significance of this
study in the discussion section (" Although the primary endpoint (ORR≥40%) was not achieved,
the 33.3% response rate substantially exceeds historical controls for anti-PD-1-refractory HCC,
which signals potential clinical utility warranting validation in larger cohorts, especially given
the limited treatment options available in this situation. ").
3. Previous retrospective experiences (e.g., Scheiner et al. JHEP Reports 2023.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhepr.2022.100620) show that ICI rechallenge in ICI-refractory
patients achieves an ORR of 26%. This is similar to the ORR showed in this manuscript, so I
am not convinced of the added value of SBRT. I would recommend modifying the discussion
accordingly.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's critical perspective regarding the added value
of SBRT in the context of ICI rechallenge efficacy. While the Scheiner et al. retrospective
analysis24 reported a 26% ORR in ICI-refractory HCC—numerically comparable to our 33.3%
ORR—several methodological distinctions necessitate cautious interpretation. Crucially, as a
prospective phase II trial, our study design inherently minimises confounding factors that
frequently challenge retrospective analyses. Upon detailed re-evaluation of the Scheiner's
cohort, two key differences emerge that may overstate ICI rechallenge efficacy:
First, 17 patients (29%) in their cohort received one or more lines of systemic therapy
between initial ICI (ICI1) and rechallenge (ICI2). These intervening treatments—potentially
including loco-regional therapies or novel agents—may have exerted immune-priming effects
analogous to radiotherapy's abscopal response, thus conflating the true rechallenge contribution.
Second, 45% of their ICI1 regimens were monotherapy (vs. only 7% in ICI2), suggesting that
enhanced efficacy during rechallenge may partly reflect intensified combination strategies
rather than the activity of rechallenge with ICI.
In contrast, our cohort exclusively enrolled patients who progressed after dual-ICI
combinations or ICI plus TKI/anti-VEGF therapy—representing a more treatment-refractory
population where prior ICI exposure was maximally optimised. Within this context, the
observed 33.3% ORR achieved with SBRT combinatorial rechallenge signals meaningful
clinical activity. We fully acknowledge that randomised trials remain essential to definitively
establish SBRT's incremental benefit, and have revised the introduction and the discussion to
incorporate:1) Comment on the rationle of Scheiner's study (JHEP Reports 2023); 2) Emphasis
on the biological plausibility of radiotherapy-induced immune sensitisation in rechallenge
settings.
We are grateful for this insightful critique, which has strengthened our manuscript's
scholarly rigor. The added discussion on objectively contextualises SBRT's potential role
within evolving ICI rechallenge paradigms.
4. The authors state that most of the patients received TKI plus anti-PD1 as first line. They
should expand on this treatment decision and clarify which agents were used, since the
international guidelines do not recognise this combination as a treatment of choice in first line
for patients with advanced HCC.
Response: We appreciate this critical inquiry regarding first-line treatment selection. The
predominant use of TKI/anti-PD-1 combinations in our cohort reflects real-world practice
patterns in China, driven by two key considerations: 1) Accessibility Constraints: The
IMbrave150 regimen (atezolizumab/bevacizumab) faces significant reimbursement barriers
and limited accessibility in China's public healthcare system; 2) Emerging Evidence: Since
2021, compelling phase II/III data from Chinese trials supported TKI/PD-1 combinations:
RESCUE Study (Clin Cancer Res. 2021): Camrelizumab + apatinib (ORR 46%), APOLLO
Trial (The LANCET Oncol 2025): Anlotinib + Penpulimab (mPFS 6.9 mo; PFS benefit vs
sorafenib, HR 0.52), and CARES-310 (THE LANCET 2023): Camrelizumab + rivoceranib
(25.4% (RECIST v1.1)/33.1% (mRECIST); PFS benefit vs sorafenib, HR 0.52). This type of
regimen received Category 1 recommendations in the CSCO HCC Guidelines from 2022. They
were more affordable than drugs imported and most of them are reimbursed by the national
health insurance. Nineteen patients were treated with at least one line of TKI plus PD-1 regimen.
Specifically, 73.7% (14/19) of these patients received a combination of lenvatinib and
camrelizumab or sintilimab, 21.1% (4/19) received apatinib and camrelizumab, and 5.3% (1/19)
received both regimens.
Per your suggestion, we have added this rationale to the results section, clarifying as "
According to the Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) guidelines, the front-line
TKI/PD-1 combination was selected based on availability and data from contemporary trials in
China, despite differences in international guidelines. "
Besides, the following was added to the Discussion: "These findings should be interpreted
considering regional therapeutic preferences. The reliance on TKI/PD-1 combinations—while
justified by local accessibility constraints and CSCO guidelines—may limit generalizability to
healthcare systems where atezolizumab/bevacizumab is first-line standard."
Thank you for highlighting this contextual nuance, we believe this clarification strengthens
the manuscript's transparency.
5. PFS was 6.2 months, while median duration of response was 5.7 months. PFS is the time
between treatment start to progression or death, so I would expect that patients responding to
the treatment have a duration of response longer than the median PFS. The authors should
clarify this point.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this vital methodological point. PFS was
defined as the time from enrolment to the first imaging of disease progression or death,
whichever occurs first; DoR: Time from first confirmed response to progression (only in
responders, see Figure R6)
Figure R6. Examples of participants' DOR
The apparent discrepancy—where median PFS (6.2 months from enrolment) exceeds
median DoR (5.7 months from first response)—stems from endpoint definitions aligned with
HCC trial standards and reflects that there is no inherent dependency requiring DoR to exceed
PFS. Notably, two patients achieved best-practice PR at the second and third evaluations,
respectively. The delay in achieving PR also led to a shortening of DOR.
6. I have some concerns regarding the treatment-related AEs. In particular, the most common
trAEs reported are decreased lymphocytes and platelets. However, these are not part of the
expected spectrum of AEs from ICI-antiVEGF. It is unlikely that this ICI combination causes a
decrease in platelets, which might be due to the underlying disease but it cannot be attributed
to an ICI combination. The authors should clarify how these AEs were considered related to the
treatment.
Response: We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewer for this perspicacious
observation regarding treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs), with particular reference to
the hematologic AEs. The attribution of decreased lymphocytes and platelets as TRAEs was
meticulously evaluated by investigators through a predefined safety assessment protocol
aligned with China NMPA's Technical Guideline for Causality Assessment of Adverse Events
in Drug Clinical Trials (2024 edition, see in the website
https://www.cde.org.cn/main/news/viewInfoCommon/0a5ae4924881321c07cce100e99f2a5c).
In order to achieve this, three core criteria had to be fulfilled: temporal plausibility
(onset/duration patterns matching known toxicity kinetics), biological gradient (dose/exposure-
dependent changes confirmed via pharmacokinetic monitoring), and exclusion of confounders
(active ruling out of disease progression, portal hypertension, and concurrent infections through
serial imaging and laboratory profiling). The specific criteria were presented in Supplementary
Table S7.
The results indicate a high proportion of TRAEs in TEAE. One potential explanation for
this phenomenon is the determination of TRAE by the investigators when the occurrence is
deemed to be a potentially treatment-related AE, as per the stipulated criteria.
In cases of lymphocyte decrease, the investigators primarily attributed these TRAEs to
sintilimab-induced T-cell exhaustion (in line with irAE patterns observed in ORIENT-329),
which may be further exacerbated by bone marrow suppression induced by stereotactic body
radiotherapy (SBRT). Regarding thrombocytopenia, the triple mechanisms of bevacizumab-
mediated inhibitory action on platelets (by suppressing sP-selectin, interfering with platelet
activation, leading to downregulation of platelet activation markers)25,26, PD-1-driven
thrombocytopenic (as documented in recent case series of immune thrombocytopenia)27 and
impaired liver function caused by treatment provided biological plausibility. Crucially, these
events manifested cyclically with treatment administration and improved upon cessation of
therapy, strengthening the causal link.
We have made the following amendments to enhance transparency in the revised
manuscript: 1) Table 2 and Supplementary Table S4 now stratifie all TRAEs and TEAEs
depending on the severity, with 3 and 4 grade separately; 2) The clarifications of TRAEs were
stated in the methods section and Supplementary Appendix includes complete causality
assessment worksheets per NMPA criteria.
7. The authors should clarify which TRAE caused the treatment discontinuation in 3 patients.
Response: Patients #4 and #5 discontinued treatment due to grade 4 gastrointestinal
haemorrhage, having completed 12 and 10 cycles of sintilimab and bevacizumab biosimilar,
respectively. Patient #11 withdrew after experiencing grade 3 anaphylaxis during her second
cycle of the same regimen. This clarification has been added to the results section as follows: "
Discontinuation of therapy occurred in 3 patients (14.3%) due to treatment-related adverse
events (TRAEs). Two cases (9.5%) of grade 4 gastrointestinal haemorrhage were observed
(Patient 4 after 12 cycles; Patient 5 after 10 cycles of sintilimab and bevacizumab biosimilar).
Both patients stabilized after endoscopic hemostasis. One participant (4.8%) of grade 3
anaphylaxis was documented (Patient 11 during cycle 2 of sintilimab and bevacizumab
biosimilar). The patient gradually recovered after treatment with corticosteroids, and sintilimab
was permanently discontinued".
8. Biomarkers analysis: how did the authors define "decline vs non decline" (line 198)?
Response: We apologise very much for the clerical error. What we actually meant to state was
that there was a difference in the PFS and OS of the patients after stratification according to the
level of plasma IFN-γ (cutoff at the median), which we have changed in the revised article to
"Survival analysis also showed that patients with a higher level of IFN-γ possessed poorer PFS
and estimated OS (Figure 3F). Median estimated OS was 24.4 months in the low-IFN-γ group
and 9.3 months in the high-IFN-γ group (Hazard Ratio [HR], 4.12; 95% CI, 1.36 - 12.46; p =
0.009). Median PFS was 7.8 months in the low-IFN-γ group and 3.7 months in the high-IFN-γ
group (HR, 3.19; 95% CI, 1.5–6.78; p = 0.025)" in result section.
9. The authors report a decrease in PDCD1 and VEGFA as biologically relevant (lines 204-205).
Maybe this is due to the targets of the anti-PD1 and the sintilimab used in the study?
Response: The points you have enumerated are highly compelling. The administration of anti-
PD1 and anti-VEGF agents has been identified as a contributing factor to this downward trend.
It is posited that a substantial decline in PDCD1 and VEGFA at the T3 time point (when the
patient exhibited optimal responses) can be discerned precisely in the patient's plasma. However,
as the disease progressed (T4 time point), although slightly, both absolute value of VEGFA and
PDCD1 increased compared to T3 (Figure R7). This indicated that monitoring plasma VEGFA
and PDCD1 abundance might facilitate disease progression prediction. However, this inference
still needs to be checked in expanded clinical samples, so we did not emphasize it in the
manuscript.
Figure R7. Expressions of PDCD1 and VEGFA tested by olink from timepoint 1 to timepoint
4. The plots and lines represent the mean and upper and lower quartiles, respectively. Paired
Wilcoxon signed rank test was used to identify significant differences. Only significant p
values (p < 0.05) were illustrated.
10. Lines 209-211: the targets increasing at progression are aspecific markers of inflammation.
It is expected they would increase in patients progressing on treatment, NLR has been
extensively studied in HCC (Wu, Cancers 2022). Same for markers in lines 221-223: the
increase in IL6 is expected after SBRT.
Response: The theory you mentioned is indeed well-established. As a typical tumour involves
an inflammation-mediated carcinogenesis process, patients with HCC, particularly in advanced
stages, are frequently already in the pathophysiological process of chronic inflammation prior
to treatment. A multitude of studies have demonstrated that specific markers of inflammation
are associated with postoperative recurrence, prognosis, and ICI resistance11,28 in hepatocellular
carcinoma. However, existing research suggests that the role of inflammatory factors in tumours
is highly heterogeneous. For instance, IL-6 can exhibit an antitumour effect in certain
circumstances, yet in others, it may stimulate tumour growth29. The time interval between T1
and T2 is very short (from enrolment to the completion of 5 fractions of SBRT), while the time
interval between T1/T2 and T4 covers the period in which most patients undergo SBRT plus
two or more cycles of systemic treatment. Previous evidence suggests that high-dose, low-
fraction SBRT has a pro-inflammatory effect and promotes antigen presentation30,31. The results
of multiple clinical studies also demonstrate that patients with Chinese hepatocellular
carcinoma caused by hepatitis B may benefit more from PD-1/PD-L1, either in combination
with anti-angiogenic or CTLA-4 antibodies32. In the context of our study, high-dose SBRT
appeared to provoke acute inflammation yet in ICI-treated HCC, which may potentiate the
antitumor efficacy of ICIs plus anti-VEGF therapy, making this rechallenge feasible. During
subsequent systemic treatment, the chronic elevation of the inflammatory factor IL-6 may
portend disease progression or resistance. However, a surprising finding was that both NLR
and PLR exhibited a gradual decline during subsequent systemic treatment (Figure R8). We
hypothesise that this may be attributable to impaired haematopoiesis and liver function, leading
to a reduction in neutrophil and platelet production in patients undergoing later-line therapy.
Therefore, NLR and PLR were inadequate as inflammatory indicators for predicting efficacy
or disease progression in our cohort. The underlying molecular mechanisms remain to be
elucidated through relevant molecular biology experiments.
Figure R8. NLR, PLR and the expressions of IL-6 tested from timepoint 1 to timepoint 4. The
plots and lines represent the mean and upper and lower quartiles, respectively. Paired
Wilcoxon signed rank test was used to identify significant differences. Only significant p
values (p < 0.05) were illustrated.*, p<0.05; **, p<0.01; ***, p<0.001.
11. Discussion: I would recommend reprhasing the first part as it does not read particularly well
(242-248)
Response: Our sincere thanks. We have revised the first paragraph of the discussion section in
response to your comments, aiming for greater conciseness and accuracy. If you remain
dissatisfied, please do not hesitate to share your specific concerns.
12. Tables: I would recommend reporting all the adverse events, not only those deemed related
to the treatment.
Response: Thanks for the advice. As recommended by you and other reviewers, we have
restructured Tables for AEs to differentiate: 1) All-grade treatment-emergent adverse events
(TEAEs) were replenished in the revised Supplementary Table S4; 2) Grade 3 and 4 treatment-
related adverse events (TRAEs), were separated listed in Table 2 (see the Criteria for Adverse
Events in Drug Clinical Trials in supplementary Table S7); 3) All TRAEs, as well as TEAEs,
are rearranged in the tables in order of decreasing incidence rate. This stratification would
distinguish event severity and attribution more precisely in the revised manuscript.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have tried to answer all questions carefully, and I do believe that all questions
about the minor limitations have been addressed. But when it comes to the major limitation, I
have to say that it cannot be solved retrospectively, it has to be considered prospectively,
when the trial was initially designed.
The most important novelty of the manuscript lies in the point that, RT remodels the TME to
“re-sensitise” the anti-PD-1 treatment, then the results from the paired clinical samples will be
absolutely pivotal.
I must say, this is still a very good work that took loads of hard work, and provide us (including
myself) very interesting clinical data and info, but this piece of missing data limits it to reach a

Response:
We are deeply grateful for your thoughtful evaluation of our work and for recognizing both the
clinical significance and inherent limitations of our study. We sincerely appreciate your
insightful synthesis regarding the clinical ontology of radiotherapy in oligoprogressive HCC—
particularly your articulation that "instead of turning immediately to later-line systemic
treatment, loco-regional therapy combined with current regimens may extend therapeutic
courses". This perspective profoundly elevates the translational relevance of our findings, and
we have integrated this concept into the revised Discussion.
Regarding the critical limitation of lacking paired tumour samples:
1. We fully concur that prospective TME biopsy integration is essential to validate radiation-
induced immune remodelling. As you rightly emphasized, "this piece of missing data limits the
mechanistic depth".
2. Immediate actions taken:
1) Added pre-treatment IHC data from 11 archival specimens (Supplementary Figure S4,
Table S6), revealing no correlation between baseline PD-L1/CD8+ T-cell density and clinical
response (*p* > 0.05). This suggests that initial TME status may not predict salvage therapy
efficacy in ICI-refractory HCC.
2) Explicitly acknowledged this limitation in the Discussion: " Critically, the absence of serial
tumour biopsies precludes direct assessment of therapy-induced TME remodelling,
diminishing translational insights."
3. Prospective validation:
1) Our ongoing phase II trial (ChiCTR2300068781) in potentially resectable HCC mandates:
pre-/post-treatment biopsies with single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics; Protocol
specifically designed to interrogate SBRT-induced changes in T-cell clonality, macrophage
polarization, and cytokine networks.
While we cannot retroactively address this limitation, your critique has fundamentally
shaped our future research trajectory. We hold your rigorous scientific standards in the highest
regard and hope that our continued work will advance this field toward precision radio-
immunotherapy.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
NCOMMS-25-10699A
The authors have successfully addressed all comments raised by the reviewers. The
improvements made to the discussion section, as well as the enhanced clarity of the figures and
tables, have significantly strengthened the overall quality of the manuscript. After careful
evaluation of the revised version, I believe this paper meets the standards for publication in
Nature Communications.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
My comments have been addressed.
Response:
We thank Reviewers #2 and #3 for their endorsement. All prior requests (e.g., statistical clarity,
figure optimization, biomarker discussion) were incorporated in the previous revision.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have provided detailed and thoughtful responses to all of my comments, and I
appreciate the clarifications and additional data included in the revised manuscript. However,
while the study is clinically interesting and the authors acknowledge its limitations, I remain
unconvinced about the added benefit of SBRT in this setting, particularly given the comparable
response rates reported in retrospective ICI rechallenge studies. I believe this question will
ultimately require validation in a randomised controlled trial.
Response:
We acknowledge that randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard to
definitively establish SBRT’s contribution. Scheiner et al.'s findings on ICI rechallenge
represent breakthrough research in this field, excitingly demonstrating that ICI rechallenge
can still achieve promising therapeutic outcomes even after resistance to immunotherapy in
HCC. Nevertheless, our data suggest that SBRT may facilitate the resensitization of immune
checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in this refractory population, a conclusion supported by two lines
of evidence:
1. Our primary endpoint evaluation was based on target lesions that had NOT been
treated with SBRT, which could reflect the systemic effects induced by SBRT. Biological
plausibility: 1) SBRT-induced cytokine surges (IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-2) were correlated with
improved PFS and response (Figure 4D–G), suggesting radiation primes antitumor immunity;
2) 100% local control of irradiated lesions highlights SBRT’s ability to eliminate local
immunosuppressive niches, potentially enabling systemic efficacy.
2. Although no head-to-head comparison was performed, our ORR, DCR, and survival
were numerically superior to those of the two ICI-resistant cohorts. We created Table R1 to
more directly compare the designs and efficacy results of different studies:
Table R1: Comparison of the data of three ICI-rechallenge cohorts.
Regorafenib +
This Study Scheiner et al.
Endpoint Pembrolizumab
(Prospective) (Retrospective)1
(Prospective)2
Sample Size 21 58 95
ORR (non-irradiated) 33.3% (7/21) 26% (15/58) 5.9–11.1%
DCR 66.7% (14/21) 55% (32/58) 40.7–51.9%
Median PFS 6.2 months 5.2 months (TTP) 4.0–4.2 months
Median OS 24.4 months 12.0 months Not reported
Indeed, neither our data nor that of the above two studies currently provides a definitive
answer, the benefits of adding SBRT in this setting still need to be further confirmed through
RCTs. Nevertheless, we can gain some insights from a series of studies on SBRT combined
with immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Paul Baas & Valsamo
Anagnostou's team has reported that combining radiotherapy with immunotherapy in patients
with NSCLC significantly increases the ORR from 20% to 50%, compared to immunotherapy
alone. It has a significant systemic immune regulatory effect, can induce a sustained immune
response, thereby improving the treatment response rate and long-term survival rate of patients
(JAMA Oncology, 2019, doi: 10.1001/jamaoncol.2019.1478; Nature Cancer, 2025, doi:
10.1038/s43018-025-01018-w). We are currently designing a randomized controlled clinical
trial to investigate the optimal timing and benefits of SBRT in patients with HCC receiving ICI
therapies. Hopefully, these trials would provide us with more evidence in this field.
We agree with your concern about overemphasizing the contribution of SBRT in this
treatment regimen. Therefore, in the revised manuscript, the emphatic language in the
discussion and conclusion sections has been replaced with more neutral, inferential descriptions
(detailed in line 291, 299 and 318 of the unmarked manuscript). Furthermore, the description
of the efficacy of SBRT in the text has been modified to refer to the combination of SBRT and
immunotherapy, as detailed in line 295, 297, and 299 of the unmarked manuscript. These
modifications will provide a more objective description of the benefits to patients in this study,
which are provided by this triple therapy regimen. We look forward to your understanding and
support for these revisions.
Also, I still think that decreased lymphocytes and platelets should not be reported as
treatment-related adverse events, because this is not in keeping with known spectrum of toxicity
from sintilimab-bevacizumab. The fact that they are reported as the most frequent trAEs raises
the question on how the toxicity data have been collected and reported in this study.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s scrutiny regarding the attribution of decreased lymphocyte
and platelet counts as TRAEs, but we respectfully disagree with the suggestion that these events
fall outside the expected spectrum for this combination regimen.
To further address your concerns, a timeline-based curve diagram of lymphocyte counts
and platelet counts was plotted for each patient (Figure R1-B, and R2-B). Interestingly, we
found that lymphopenia is likely closely associated with SBRT, as we did observe transient
lymphocyte decreases or upgraded AE ratings in most patients following SBRT.
Figure R1-B. The counts of lymphocytes reported by blood routine test of all 8 patients who
experienced lymphocytopenia. Triangles: Self-reported cold (possible viral infection); LLN,
lower limit of normal. The Blue squares represented the timing of the first report of TRAE.
Figure R2-B. The counts of platelets reported by blood routine test and the symptomatic
treatment of all 8 patients who experienced thrombocytopenia. LLN, lower limit of normal.
The Blue squares represented the timing of the first report of TRAE.
In addition to the temporal association between treatment and adverse events (AEs), there
is mechanistic evidence supporting the classification of these phenomena as TRAEs.
Specifically, SBRT is a well-documented cause of lymphopenia, as demonstrated in the
literature on combined modality therapy (SBRT is a well-established cause of lymphopenia,
supported by literature in combined modality therapy (e.g., Li, et al., 2024, Nature
Communications3; Paganetti, 2023, Frontiers in Oncology4; Chen et al., 2023, World J
Gastroenterol5). The significant post-SBRT drop in lymphocytes observed in our cohort
(Figure R1-B and Figure R2-B) strongly supports this mechanism. Furthermore, the regimen
combining bevacizumab and sintilimab is known to impact platelet levels, with an incidence
rate of approximately 26% reported in the ORIENT-326, which is comparable to the 38%
observed in our study. These findings suggest that the novel triplet combination therapy may
exert synergistic or additive hematologic effects, contributing to the observed AEs.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) poses a major therapeutic challenge. Here we present a Phase 2 trial evaluating stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) combined with sintilimab and bevacizumab biosimilar (PD-1/VEGF blockade) to overcome resistance in ICI-refractory HCC. Twenty-one patients with progressive HCC after ICI therapy receive SBRT followed by sintilimab 200 mg and bevacizumab biosimilar 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks. The primary outcome, objective response rate in non-irradiated lesions is 33.3%, with a disease control rate of 66.7%. Median progression-free survival is 6.2 months, and estimated median overall survival is 24.4 months. SBRT achieves 100% local control, with 33.3% experiencing grade 3 or higher adverse events. Proteomic profiling reveals that responders exhibit lower baseline IFN-γ and elevated IL-6, while post-SBRT increases in IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-6 correlate with improved outcomes. These results indicate that combination of SBRT in ICI-refractory HCC is effective, well-tolerated, and may be guided by cytokine assessment.

---

## Introduction

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for 90% of all primary liver cancers; it ranks as the third leading cause of cancer-related death globally1, with an estimated 5-year survival rate of less than 4% for advanced-stage patients2. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), particularly anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agents, have revolutionised systemic therapy, enabling durable responses in a subset of patients3. However, monotherapy yields limited objective response rates (ORRs) of 13–20% (e.g., durvalumab4 and tislelizumab5). Consequently, combination strategies integrating ICIs with antiangiogenic agents (anti-VEGF agents, e.g., bevacizumab), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), or anti-CTLA-4 antibodies have emerged as first-line standards. Landmark phase 3 trials, including IMbrave150 (atezolizumab plus bevacizumab; ORR 27.3%6), ORIENT-32 (sintilimab plus bevacizumab biosimilar; ORR 21.0%7), CARES-310 (camrelizumab plus rivoceranib; ORR 26.8%8), HIMALAYA (tremelimumab plus durvalumab; ORR 20.1%4), and CheckMate-9DW (nivolumab plus ipilimumab; ORR 36%9), have demonstrated significantly improved outcomes over sorafenib or lenvatinib.

Despite these advances, at least 60% of patients receive no benefit from combination immunotherapy (IO), and the inevitable immunoresistance remains a formidable constraint to implementing ICIs4,6,8. These patients then become candidates for next-line treatment. Treatment options after progression on front-line ICI regimens remain poorly defined, as most approved second-line agents (e.g., regorafenib) have been validated in sorafenib-pretreated populations10. Currently, the choice for late-line therapy after front- or second-line ICI treatment is primarily empirical, with the shift between ICIs and anti-angiogenic agents largely dependent on drug safety, patient comorbidities, physician and patient preferences, and local reimbursement policies.

Currently, data are available from several retrospective studies exploring the feasibility and efficacy of rechallenging with ICIs in the context of prior exposure11–13. However, the protocols have mainly focused on the use of different ICI combinations and the replacement of previously unused ICI-based regimens. The main rationale is that inhibiting non-cross-resistance might promote antitumour responses in patients who did not respond to previous ICI therapy14–16. These types of regimens are reported to have tolerable toxicity, with ORRs ranging from 16–30% and disease control rates (DCRs) ranging from 40%–55%11–13. The therapeutic effectiveness of a simply substituted immunotherapy category remains unsatisfactory, yet prospective data are scarce.

In addition to systemic therapy, locoregional therapies, such as radioembolization and radiotherapy, have been explored and are promising, with favourable results17,18. Radiotherapy has rapidly become a crucial component of multidisciplinary treatment for liver cancer due to advances in technology, resulting in the transition to stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT)19. SBRT allows high doses of radiation to be applied to the targeted tumour area in a limited number of fractions with less damage to the surrounding healthy tissues. Recent prospective and retrospective studies have reported that SBRT can achieve high rates of local tumour control at 2 years, ranging from 68–95%20,21, and is an effective local treatment for inoperable early-, intermediate-, and advanced-stage HCCs19. However, many patients experience out-of-field progression, highlighting the need for concurrent systemic disease control22.

Accumulating evidence has demonstrated that radiotherapy rewires the tumour microenvironment (TME) to enhance immunotherapeutic sensitivity through dual mechanisms: stimulating tumour cells to upregulate immune-recognition molecules that potentiate cancer cell detection and antitumour immune activation23–27 while concurrently inducing pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that recruit effector immune cells into the TME24,28. Consequently, SBRT is being actively investigated in combination with systemic agents, particularly ICIs, for the treatment of metastatic lesions across multiple malignancies, including HCC29. Antiangiogenic therapies such as VEGF inhibitors further augment this approach by demonstrating radiosensitizing properties in tumours such as glioma30 and potentiating radiation-induced abscopal effects when combined with ICIs in HCC31. Nevertheless, whether SBRT-mediated tumoral or circulating immune microenvironment reprogramming can resensitize patients with immunotherapy-refractory HCC to subsequent ICI regimens remains an unanswered clinical question.

Herein, we report the results of the ReUNION-1 study, a phase 2 trial of sintilimab (IBI308) and a bevacizumab biosimilar (IBI305) combined with SBRT after failure of anti-PD-1 treatment in patients with unresectable HCC. In light of the need to identify potential biomarkers and clarify the basis of the tumour response, we analysed serial blood samples obtained before treatment and at time points during treatment and identified many SBRT-induced and efficacy-correlated cytokines. This study will provide evidence for the efficacy of combining SBRT with ICI in patients with ICI-refractory HCC.

---

## Results

Patient characteristics
The trial schema is summarised in Fig. 1A and Supplementary Fig. S1A. Between March 2022 and April 2024, a total of 25 patients were screened for eligibility. Among them, one patient had no target lesion other than the proposed radiotherapy lesion; two patients underwent gastroscopy, suggesting untreated or incompletely treated oesophageal or gastric varices with bleeding or a high risk of bleeding; and one patient declined enrolment for personal reasons. Ultimately, 21 patients were enroled (Fig. 1B). The baseline demographics of the patients are summarised in Supplementary Dataset 1 and Supplementary Dataset 2. All 21 patients were included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, with a cut-off date of 31 August 2024 (Fig. 1B). The median duration of the latest line immunotherapy before enrolment was 7.4 months (interquartile range [IQR], 5.9–18.4 months). The median age was 55 years, and 81.0% of the patients were men. Nine patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 0, and 12 had a PS of 1. All 21 patients had a Child-Pugh grade of A at baseline. According to the Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) guidelines, the front-line TKI/PD-1 combination was selected based on availability and data from contemporary trials in China, despite differences in international guidelines. Nineteen patients were treated with at least one line of TKI plus PD-1. Specifically, 73.7% (14/19) of these patients received a combination of lenvatinib and camrelizumab or sintilimab, 21.1% (4/19) received apatinib and camrelizumab, and 5.3% (1/19) received both regimens. Additionally, one patient received anti-VEGF (bevacizumab) plus anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab) treatment, and another received anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1 treatment. Details of the fractionation regimen for each patient receiving SBRT treatment (median dose 8 Gy/fraction, range 5–8 Gy in 5 fractions) and the target lesion dose-volume metrics used to assess efficacy, including the median volume receiving ≥5 Gy (V5, which was 0%), can be found in the Source data. Chronic HBV infection was the leading cause of liver disease (n=18, 85.7%). Most patients were characterised by the following: prior one-line systemic therapy (n=13, 61.9%), high baseline serum AFP levels (n=12, 57.1%), multiple intrahepatic lesions (n=18, 85.7%), and extrahepatic metastasis (n=15, 71.5%).

Treatment efficacy
With a median follow-up of 9.1 months (IQR, 7.6–16.1), 21 (100%) of the 21 patients were evaluable for the best overall response (BOR). A confirmed partial response (PR) was observed in 7 patients without complete response (CR), contributing to an ORR of 33.3%. Stable disease (SD) was observed in 7 patients, with a DCR of 66.7% (Fig. 2A and Table 1). Notably, reductions in the sizes of irradiated lesions after treatment compared with those at baseline were observed in 20 (95.2%) of the 21 enrolled patients (Fig. 2B). The local-regional control (LRC) rate was 100% (21/21, Fig. 2B), indicating excellent local control of SBRT treatment. Excitingly, lesions outside the irradiation field can also achieve very effective results (Supplementary Fig. S2A, S2B). Durable disease control, defined as continuous tumour control lasting ≥6 months, was observed in patients with both a PR and SD. One patient with a PR according to RECIST v1.1 maintained disease control for more than two years after IBI cessation. Three of the seven patients who experienced a PR remained alive, with no alternative systemic therapy required. Seven patients had progressive disease as their best response.

By the data cut-off date for the final analysis, 18 patients experienced disease progression, the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 6.2 months (Fig. 2C, D, 95% CI: 3.7–15.1 months), and 2 patients were still under treatment (Fig. 2C). The 6-month and 12-month PFS rates were 57.1% (95% CI, 36.5%–75.5%) and 14.3% (95% CI, 5.0%–34.6%), respectively (Fig. 2D). Additionally, eight patients died, and the estimated median overall survival (OS) was 24.4 months (Fig. 2C, D, 95% CI: 9.2 months-NA). Kaplan-Meier estimates of the 6-month and 12-month OS rates were 95.2% (95% CI 77.3%–99.8%) and 33.3% (95% CI 17.2%–54.6%), respectively. The median duration of response (mDOR) was 5.70 months (95% CI, 2.0–12.4). Overall, local responses were strong and durable (Fig. 2E, F, Supplementary Fig. S2B). Moreover, neither the location of the metastases nor the response to prior ICI therapy nor PFS to prior ICI therapy was significantly associated with treatment response or clinical benefit (Supplementary Fig. S2C, S2D, Supplementary Table S1), indicating the generalisability of this regimen among HCC patients who were refractory to immunotherapy.

Safety
All patients included in the ITT analysis completed radiotherapy and at least one cycle of sequential treatment with sintilimab plus a bevacizumab biosimilar. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) and treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) are listed in Table 2 and Supplementary Table S2, respectively. During the therapy period, TRAEs of any grade occurred in 17 of 21 patients (81.0%; see details in Table 2). No unexpected adverse events or treatment-related deaths occurred. Commonly observed TRAEs included decreased lymphocyte count (n=8, 38.1%), decreased platelet count (n=8, 38.1%), and increased alanine aminotransferase (n=8, 38.1%) and aspartate aminotransferase (n=8, 38.1%). Grade 3 or higher TRAEs (serious TRAEs) occurred in 7 (33.3%) patients, commonly including decreased platelet count (n=2, 9.5%), decreased white blood cell count, neutropenia (n=2, 9.5%), decreased platelet count (n=2, 9.5%), and gastrointestinal haemorrhage (n=2, 9.5%). Discontinuation of therapy occurred in 3 patients (14.3%) due to serious TRAEs. Two cases (9.5%) of grade 4 gastrointestinal haemorrhage were observed (Patient 4 after 12 cycles; Patient 5 after 10 cycles of sintilimab and bevacizumab biosimilar). Both patients stabilised after endoscopic haemostasis. One participant (4.8%) with grade 3 anaphylaxis was documented (Patient 11 during cycle 2 of sintilimab and bevacizumab biosimilar). The patient gradually recovered after treatment with corticosteroids, and sintilimab was permanently discontinued. One patient (4.8%) with withdrew from the trial due to personal preference.

Biomarkers for treatment response and outcomes
Serial Olink proteomics assays for Immuno-Oncology in plasma (see details in Supplementary Dataset 3 and Supplementary Dataset 4), in parallel with flow cytometry analysis for immune lineages in PBMCs, were performed to compare responders and non-responders to identify possible biomarkers that could predict efficacy. A total of 52 samples were obtained and tested at the time points indicated in Supplementary Fig. S1. All samples passed quality control and were included in the analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3A).

At the T1 time point, responders (Rs, defined as patients with PR) exhibited significantly lower enrichment of IFN-γ (p=0.025) and serum globulin (GLB, p=0.047) and higher levels of CXCL1 (p=0.036), TNF-α (p=0.048), and IL-6 (p=0.002) than non-responders (NRs, defined as patients with SD and PD; Fig. 3A, D, Supplementary Fig. S3B-C and S3G). Additionally, responders had a significantly higher percentage of CD4+ T cells (p=0.019), white blood cell (WBC) count (p=0.038), albumin-to-globulin ratios (A/G, p=0.025), and neutrophil count (p=0.046) than non-responders (Supplementary Fig. S3D and S3G). When the duration of response was considered, IFN-γ expression (p=0.014) and AFP levels (p=0.007) were lower in patients with clinical benefit response (CBR, patients with SD longer than 6 months and patients with PR) than in non clinical benefit (NCB) patients (patients with SD less than 6 months and patients with progression disease [PD]), whereas VEGFA (p=0.033), TWEAK (p=0.026), CD4 (p=0.049), IL-6 (p=0.043), and TNF-α (p=0.0031) levels were higher (Fig. 3B, D, Supplementary Fig. S3B and S3H). Additional biomarkers or characteristics, including age, sex, ECOG score, China liver cancer (CNLC) staging, enrichment of immune lineages, and serum AFP levels, were analysed for correlation with clinical efficacy (Supplementary Fig. S3I). Unsurprisingly, the levels of the classical tumour biomarker AFP were consistently lower in patients with CBR and long PFS at baseline.

Intriguingly, levels of plasma IFN-γ were also decreased in patients with longer PFS than in those with shorter PFS (p=0.0058, Fig. 3C, D). Survival analysis also showed that patients with a higher level of IFN-γ had poorer PFS and estimated OS (Fig. 3F). The median estimated OS was 24.4 months in the low-IFN-γ group and 9.3 months in the high-IFN-γ group (hazard ratio [HR], 4.12; 95% CI, 1.36–12.46; p=0.009). The median PFS was 7.8 months in the low-IFN-γ group and 3.7 months in the high-IFN-γ group (HR, 3.19; 95% CI, 1.5–6.78; p=0.025). Moreover, the existence of extrahepatic metastases (EHS) was correlated with shorter PFS (HR, 5.62; 95% CI: 1.23–25.62) but was not significantly correlated with a lower ORR (EHS vs. non-EHS: 26.7% vs. 50%, p=0.354), and AFP<400 μg/L was correlated with better PFS (HR, 0.09; 95% CI: 0.02–0.41) (Fig. 3E, F, Supplementary Fig. S3J and S3L).

We further investigated the dynamics of plasma proteins in patients at the time of BOR and disease progression. The results demonstrated a downward trend in the expression of PDCD1 (p=0.02) and VEGFA (p=0.0003), as well as in the ratio of CD4+ T cells to CD8+ T cells (Th/Ts, p=0.002). In contrast, an increase in the abundance of CD8+ T cells (p=0.006) and the ratio of terminal effector T cells (defined as CD45RA+CCR7-CD8+ T cells) to CD8+ T cells (p=0.031) was observed when the patients achieved BOR (Fig. 3I), irrespective of response. Impressively, when the disease progressed, the expression levels of arginase 1 (ARG1) and placental growth factor (PGF) and the neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) significantly increased compared with those at baseline, whereas the levels of the T-cell activation marker OX-40 and the T-cell chemotactic factor CX3CL1 significantly decreased (Fig. 3J).

Dynamics of cytokines and immune cells in the circulation during SBRT
Subsequently, we enumerated the differences in the levels of circulating immune cells and immuno-oncology-related proteins before and after SBRT (Fig. 4). A significant SBRT-induced increase in IL15, IL6, and CD70 and a decline of VEGFA, B cells, and total lymphocytes were detected. After SBRT, the median frequency of B cell and lymphocyte counts in unirradiated PBMCs decreased from 12.01% (IQR 8.92–15.72%) to 7.46% (IQR 4.35–11.11%) (p=0.0017) and from 1.26 (IQR 0.96–1.75) G/L to 0.73 (IQR 0.46–1.14) G/L (p=0.016), respectively, and the circulating abundance of VEGFA decreased from 9.68 (IQR 9.26–9.94) to 9.28 (IQR 9.04–9.59) (p=0.0057). In contrast, the concentrations of circulating IL6 (3.756 versus 3.278, p=0.0442), CD70 (4.090 versus 3.872, p=0.0088), and IL15 (4.413 versus 4.030, p=0.0091) and two other specific inflammatory markers, the NLR (3.644 versus 2.090, p=0.0043) and the PLR (202.7 versus 111.2, p=0.0058), were significantly elevated after SBRT (Fig. 4A, C, Supplementary Fig. S4A).

While our findings indicated that radiotherapy-induced perturbations in plasma cytokine profiles and immune cell subsets were associated with therapeutic response and PFS, only variations displaying consistent statistical significance across subgroup analyses were deemed to hold substantive relevance to clinical efficacy (Fig. 4A, C). Specifically, SBRT triggered a more prominent augmentation in plasma concentrations of IFN-γ, IL-6, and IL-17A in the CBR group and long-term survival patients (Fig. 4D, E, G) than in the NCB group and patients with short PFS. Additionally, a higher expression of IL-2 in post-SBRT plasma was associated with a better response to the ICI-combined treatment (Fig. 4D, F, G). Moreover, a more pronounced decrease in circulating MMP12 in pre-SBRT and post-SBRT blood samples was associated with improved PFS and clinical benefit (Fig. 4D, E, G). Taken together, inflammation signalling, such as via IFN-γ, IL-6, and IL-2, might be particularly essential in mediating SBRT-triggered immune responses.

Other biomarkers and subgroup analysis
Additional biomarkers or characteristics, including age, sex, ECOG score, prior lines of treatment, expression of PD-L1, infiltration by CD8+ T and CD4+ T cells at diagnosis, existence of liver metastasis, and serum PIVKA-II levels, were analysed for correlation with clinical efficacy (Figure S4B, S4C, Supplementary Table S1, and Supplementary Dataset 1), and no significant differences were observed.

## Methods

Study design and participants
The open-label, single-arm, phase 2 study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and all patients provided written informed consent before enrolment. The institutional review boards of Wuhan Union Hospital approved the study (Ethics number: [2022] 0136-01). The trial was registered with chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2200056068) on 31 January 2022, and the published study protocol59 was provided in the Supplementary Information. Analyses were conducted as planned in the preregistration. Patients did not receive financial compensation for participation in the study.

Patients aged 18 years or over with an ECOG performance status of ≤1 and clinically or pathologically diagnosed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that had failed to respond to previous anti-PD-1 immunotherapy were eligible for enrolment. According to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumour version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1), measurable disease was required if at least one tumour was amenable to SBRT treatment at a dose of 25–50 Gy in 5 fractions, and another measurable tumour lesion was present that did not undergo radiotherapy for efficacy assessment.

Other inclusion criteria included having an A Child-Pugh grade, a life expectancy of ≥3 months, and sufficient bone marrow and organ function. The exclusion criteria included a history of any other malignancy, metastases to the central nervous system, previous radiotherapy, autoimmune or interstitial lung disease, or serious comorbidities, such as congestive heart failure or uncontrolled diabetes.

Procedures
Patients underwent SBRT once daily for five consecutive days, targeting a single tumour lesion. Sintilimab (200 mg, Innovent Biologics, Suzhou, China) combined with bevacizumab biosimilar (15 mg/kg, Innovent Biologics, Suzhou, China) was administered intravenously every 3 weeks, starting 1–2 weeks after completion of SBRT. Treatment continued until disease progression, the occurrence of intolerable toxicity, patient withdrawal, death, or for a maximum duration of 24 months. All patients included in the ITT analysis had finished radiotherapy and at least one cycle of sequential treatment with sintilimab plus a bevacizumab biosimilar. Complete follow-up, including physical examination, information on adverse events, and radiographic evaluation, was performed every 9 weeks. Key laboratory tests and flow cytometry analysis of immune lineages in PBMCs were performed in the clinical laboratory of Wuhan Union Hospital.

Outcomes
The primary endpoint was the ORR, defined as the percentage of patients who had a RECIST v1.1-defined CR or PR; only non-irradiated (abscopal) lesions were RECIST eligible60. The secondary endpoints included DCR, PFS (time from the date of enrolment to the date of disease progression or death), OS (time from the date of enrolment to the date of death), and LRC rates. The PFS or OS times of patients who were still progression-free or alive at the time of the last follow-up were censored. Responders (Rs) were defined as patients with BOR of PR. Non-responders (NRs) were defined as patients with BOR of SD or PD. Clinical benefit responders (CBR) were defined as patients who achieved a BOR of PR or SD lasting longer than 6 months. Non-clinical benefit (NCB) was defined as patients with a BOR of PD or SD lasting less than 6 months. Long progression-free survival (LPFS) and short progression-free survival (SPFS) were defined as patients with PFS longer or shorter than the median PFS, respectively. LRC rates were defined as the proportion of patients without local progression of all irradiated target lesions from the baseline value according to the RECIST 1.1 assessment. Outfield lesions were defined as lesions outside the 500 cGy dosimetric line. The safety assessment spanned from informed consent through follow-up. Investigators evaluated adverse event (AE) incidence and severity per the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. AEs, including TEAEs, TRAEs and serious TRAEs, were monitored during treatment and up to 30 days after the last dose according to the study protocol. TRAEs were meticulously evaluated by investigators through a safety assessment protocol aligned with China NMPA’s Technical Guideline for Causality Assessment of Adverse Events in Drug Clinical Trials (2024 edition, https://www.cde.org.cn/main/news/viewInfoCommon/0a5ae4924881321c07cce100e99f2a5c). Three core criteria had to be fulfilled: temporal plausibility (onset/duration patterns matching known toxicity kinetics), biological gradient (dose/exposure-dependent changes confirmed via pharmacokinetic monitoring), and the exclusion of confounders (active ruling out disease progression, portal hypertension, and concurrent infection through serial imaging and laboratory profiling). The specific criteria are presented in Supplementary Dataset 5.

Plasma immune proteomics
Plasma samples were collected at the indicated time points according to the timeline described in Supplementary Fig. 1A, 1B. The main time points include baseline (T1) after SBRT and before IBIstreatment (T2), at best overall response (T3), and at disease progression (T4). All samples were tested in a single run in the same batch. Proteins in the plasma samples were measured using the Olink® Target Immuno-Oncology Panel (Olink Proteomics, Sweden) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, which includes the detection of 92 proteins by the proximity expansion assay (PEA) with 1 μL of each sample. In brief, pairs of oligonucleotide-labelled antibody probes bind to their target proteins. If the two probes come into proximity, their oligonucleotides hybridise in a pairwise manner.

The introduction of DNA polymerase initiates a proximity-dependent DNA polymerisation event, generating a unique PCR target sequence. This sequence is subsequently detected and quantified using a microfluidic real-time PCR instrument (Biomark HD, Fluidigm). The resulting Ct data undergo quality control and normalisation against a set of internal and external controls. The final assay output is reported as normalised protein expression (NPX) values, which are arbitrary units on a log2 scale, where higher values indicate greater protein expression. The four internal controls are designed to emulate and monitor the distinct stages of the PEA process. These include two incubation/immuno controls, an extension control, and a detection control. The internal controls are added to all samples as well as to the external controls, serving for quality assurance and data normalisation. The external controls comprise a negative control, which is utilised for determining the limit of detection (LOD), and triplicate interplate controls (IPCs), which are used for data normalisation.

Quality control of the data occurs in two stages. First, the run’s quality is assessed by calculating the standard deviation for both the detection control and the incubation/immuno controls. For a run to pass quality control, this standard deviation must be less than 0.2. Second, each sample undergoes quality control by comparing its detection control and one of the incubation control results against the run median. All assay validation data, including detection limits and intra- and inter-assay precision data, are available on the manufacturer’s website (www.olink.com). The complete dataset for the Olink analysis has been uploaded as Supplementary Dataset 4.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis of the tumour immune microenvironment
We analysed 11 FFPE samples from pre-enrolled HCC primary or metastatic lesions: (a) 9 primary HCCs (8 surgical resections, 1 ultrasound-guided biopsy) and (b) 2 lung metastases (1 metastasectomy, 1 CT-guided biopsy). Tissues were collected at Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (from 2019–2023; see details in Source data) with histopathological confirmation. IHC analysis was performed on 4-μm FFPE sections using antibodies against CD4 (Clone 4B12, Dako #M7310), CD8 (Clone C8/144B, Dako #M7103), and PD-L1 (Clone 22C3, Dako #SK006). Following EDTA-based antigen retrieval (pH 9.0, 95°C, 20 min) and overnight primary antibody incubation at 4°C, the sections were stained with EnVision FLEX/HRP (Dako) and DAB, and haematoxylin was used for counterstaining. The quantitative assessment included the following: 1) CD4+/CD8+ T-cell density (cells/mm²) counted in five random 400× HPFs spanning intratumoural and invasive margin regions and 2) PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) = PD-L1+ cells (tumour/lymphocytes/macrophages)/viable tumour cells × 100 (CPS≥1=positive, per the FDA 22C3 pharmDx criteria). Experienced pathologists performed all assessments.

Statistical analysis
This trial adopted Simon’s two-stage optimal design to evaluate the primary endpoint of ORR. Historical benchmarks defined the null (π₀=15%)7 and alternative (π₁=40%) response hypotheses. Early termination criteria stipulated trial discontinuation if ≤1 response occurred among the initial 9 evaluable participants (stage I). Progression to stage II disease required ≥2 responses, with final efficacy declared if >5/19 patients achieved responses (α=0.05, power=80%). To account for 10% attrition, 21 patients were enrolled.

The efficacy-evaluable population comprised participants who received ≥1 treatment cycle with post-baseline imaging. The safety analysis included all patients who were administered ≥1 dose with follow-up toxicity assessments. Survival endpoints (PFS/OS) were analysed via Kaplan-Meier estimates with log-rank tests, whereas response rates (ORRs/DCRs) were calculated using Clopper-Pearson exact 95% CIs—Cox proportional hazard models generated HRs for survival comparisons.

For further analysis, subgroup comparisons between responders and non-responders were conducted using the exact Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The relationship between potential biomarkers and the radiographic response was assessed via Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. Additionally, biomarker levels before and after treatment were compared using the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test to evaluate treatment effects. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for intergroup comparisons. Correlations between biomarkers were quantified via Spearman’s ρ, with longitudinal changes assessed using the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. All analyses were conducted bidirectionally (SPSS Statistics 26; R, version 4.3.1) at p<0.05, with visualisation implemented in R and GraphPad Prism 9. Data analysis of proteomics was conducted using the Olink NPX Signature Software (version 1.16.0) for quality control (QC) of Olink data.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
